1.1: 1.1 Argument. He instructs Timothy and teaches him about the ordination of the episcopate and the diaconate, and of all ecclesiastical discipline, writing to him from Laodicea by Tychicus the deacon.
1.2: 1.2 Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father. In this greeting he puts three things which he desires, whereas in others he has put only two. Mercy is here taken for what in other epistles is called grace, that is, the remission of sins. Peace is tranquillity of soul, a foretaste of eternal peace. This is commonly wished for all. But grace, which he adds here, is wished for bishops, that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the ministers of God are armed.
1.3: 1.3 As I besought you. After the greeting he first speaks of repelling the false teachers: here he begins with those who still teach that the law must be kept. I besought. AMBROSE. He says I besought, to show the affection of charity and the pattern of humility. Fables and genealogies. AUGUSTINE, book II against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, ch. 1. A certain heretic, an enemy of the law and the prophets, supposes that the Apostle in this place called the divine oracles fables, etc., down to which sacred Scripture nowhere narrates.
1.4: 1.4 Genealogies. These were genealogies by which certain Jews told that they were of the race of Abraham and David, as though something were owed to them on that account, or by which they told that Christ was not descended from David.
1.5: 1.5 Now the end. In faith is the building of God, because from faith is hope, and from that charity, which is the fulfilling of the law. Or construe thus: Some teach and attend to fables and genealogies, but the end and fulfilling of the law is charity, wherefore there is no need of other things. Of the precept. Precept is put for precepts, whose fulfilling is the love of God and neighbor. Hence: On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets, Matthew 22. AUGUSTINE, on Psalm 31. End is said to be a limit, etc., down to let covetousness therefore be curbed, charity stirred up. A good conscience. Conscience for hope. For he despairs of reaching what he loves who has the scruple of a bad conscience within. And faith unfeigned. Or, not made of clay and fragile, or, in which not each man fashions for himself whatever he likes, but only the catholic faith.
1.6: 1.6 From which. Here he condemns the adversaries who handed on legal observances. Not understanding, etc. For whenever they begin to be reproved and convicted of their perverse and false opinion, to defend what they said with the lightest rashness and plainest falsehood they pronounce many words from the holy books, wishing to be teachers of the law, though they do not understand what they say, or about what.
1.8: 1.8 But we know. Lest he seem to accuse the law, he adds: But we know, etc. But lest he seem again to bring it in, he subjoins: Knowing this, that the law is not made for the just man: because he is not just from it, but from faith. For what then is the law necessary to him? It was given in order either to punish the guilty or to restrain him who wished to sin. The just man, however, even if he does not need it, uses it, so that he might be in authority to others, and might attest by deeds the things to come. Use it lawfully. He who knows the law was given for a time and abandons it under Christ. The just now have no need of the law, from which they are free through Christ. But there are many ways of using the law lawfully, so that in one respect a just man and in another an unjust one may rightly be said to use the law lawfully. For the unjust man uses it lawfully when, understanding why it was given, he is led by its threatening, as by a tutor, to grace, by which he may become just. The just man, however, also uses it lawfully, when by holding to it he lays it upon the unjust, so that when, with the incentive of prohibition and the accumulation of transgression, the disease of ingrained concupiscence begins to grow in them, they flee to justifying grace, and, delighted by the sweetness of righteousness through it, escape the punishment of the threatening letter.
1.12: 1.12 I give thanks to him who, etc. Here he shows that the law had evils for him, but the good things were these, once it was set aside: that he is faithful and placed in the ministry, whence also strong: by which he shows that after the Gospel the law is led in uselessly.
1.13: 1.13 But I obtained mercy. Those obtain mercy who sin knowingly, as David, and those who sin ignorantly, which is more easily pardoned. I obtained mercy from this, that I acted ignorantly. Or ignorance is set down as the cause of mercy, though not properly, since the ignorance was bad, but the mercy gratuitous.
1.14: 1.14 It abounded. Above greater goods than formerly evils. Because he not only forgave sins, but gave faith and love. About which no one is to doubt: That Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners. And this saying is faithful, that is true and acceptable, because useful.
1.15: 1.15 Worthy of all acceptance, because it saves body and soul. Or, this saying is human. Another reading: not to say divine, because if a man who receives a man into hospitality is called humane, how much more humane is he who receives man into himself. That Christ Jesus. Christ had no cause of coming except to save sinners. The chief. That is the worse, because a persecutor, than whom none was prior: for none was fiercer among persecutors, therefore none prior among sinners; he was first therefore not in order of time but in greatness of iniquity.
1.16: 1.16 But for this cause I obtained mercy, etc. Otherwise he judges that he obtained mercy for this reason: that no sinner, pressed by whatever crimes, should now despair of himself, but rather presume to obtain the same pardon by this example: the gift is very great and truly immense. In me. Whom God appointed a fit preacher to the Gentiles, in whom he showed so great an example of his mercy.
1.17: 1.17 Invisible. Because the other gods are visible. He is not said to be the only invisible one, because there are also certain invisible creatures, such as the soul, which can nevertheless be grasped by sense: because all its powers can be known, but it is not God to us. God is therefore invisible by nature to men, according to that: No man has seen God at any time. But he is seen when he wills and as he wills, not as he is, but he wills to appear in a kind of appearance. In the future, however, his children will see him as he is. To the only God. Who alone is God by nature, that is, alone creates, which is understood of the Trinity itself, not of the Father alone, as some wish: because he does not say, to the only Father, but to the only God. For the Trinity itself is preached by us as one and the only God. And the Only-begotten, according as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit in his nature are immortal and invisible.
1.18: 1.18 This precept. After he has recalled what and how great are the benefits of the Father and of Christ toward sinners, he shows how he is to instruct the people in ecclesiastical discipline.
1.19: 1.19 Conscience. He calls thoughts by that name, in which humility is to be preserved above all, and some, having spurned it, have fallen into great errors, as was shown at the beginning of the epistle to the Romans.
1.20: 1.20 Whom I delivered. The Apostle excommunicated both, so that in this way the kingdom of Satan might be shut out by Satan. For there is no creature, whether one that abides in truth giving glory to God, or one that did not stand in charity seeking its own glory, which, willing or unwilling, does not serve divine providence. But the willing one does with it what is good. Of the one that does not will this, what is just is done. Yet what is justly done concerning it is not repaid to it, but only in what spirit it itself acts, because God has not denied free will to the rational creature, but has retained the power by which he justly orders the unjust. Delivered. Not however so that they perish, because Satan can do nothing unless permitted, who vexes those given to him; whence: Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you, John 5. Thus the apostolic power itself used Satan for the correction of men. For the prevaricating angels with their prince the devil are rightly called procurators, or agents of divine providence, and the devil is called the magistrate of this world, but a magistrate under God the emperor, who does nothing except as much as is permitted him, and the procurators and agents of this world do nothing except as much as the Lord allows.
2.1: 2.1 I beseech. So far about the false apostles, here about prayers. First of all. That is, before all things that supplications be made. The order of the Mass is shown here, which is a special kind of prayer. Supplications. Either the prayer which is made near or before the consecration. Prayers. That is, the consecration itself. Petitions. Or intercessions, as if from debt, that what is done here may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people is blessed by the bishop. Thanksgivings. For deeds done, which conclude the whole as though the whole were from God: that we may bless the Lord. For all men. That we may follow the clemency of God, because God wills all men to be saved, although according to justice he reprobates some. That we may lead a quiet life, free from persecution.
2.3: 2.3 For this. Lest anyone think these things are not to be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: For this is good. And lest anyone think that salvation could be had by the worship of one God and a good life without participation in the body of Christ, that is, without the faith of the Church. There is one God, he says, and one mediator, so that all men may be saved never happens except through the mediator, God the Word who always was, yet according to the flesh was made.
2.4: 2.4 Mediator of God, etc. This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: Would that there were an arbiter between us. AUGUSTINE, book IX of the City of God, ch. 15. A mediator between God and men, it was fitting that he have something like God, etc., down to another, good, who reconciles enemies, Jesus Christ.
2.7: 2.7 And truth. The future truth is the thing and reward of faith. Do you seek the reward? Let faith go first. For we believe in order to know, we do not know in order to believe. For what is faith, if not to believe what you do not see? Faith therefore is to believe what you do not see. Truth, to see what you have believed.
2.8: 2.8 I will therefore that men, etc. AUGUSTINE, sermon 93 on the Season. Christ lifted up his hands for us on the cross, etc., down to that your own works may come to your mind. Wrath is toward the neighbor; disputing, toward God.
2.9: 2.9 Not with braided hair, etc. Let them not, in all these things, beyond the measure of their station and manners, strive to give occasion for stirring up desire, but rather by all good works be promising and showing godliness of soul outwardly.
2.11: 2.11 Let the woman in silence. He said the duty of praying belongs to all, and how, and for whom, and why, and that it is to be done everywhere. Now he says that the office of teaching belongs to men alone, and determines what sort of men ought to be ordained to it.
2.12: 2.12 To teach, etc. Behold, he has not only taught that a woman should have a humble and honest bearing, but has also denied her the authority of teaching, and commanded her to be subject to the man, so that in both bearing and obedience she be under the power of the man from whom she draws her origin.
2.14: 2.14 Adam was not. AUGUSTINE, book II on Genesis according to the letter, last ch. Since the Apostle calls her a transgressor in the likeness of Adam's transgression, etc., down to I think he could in no way have been deceived.
2.15: 2.15 She shall be saved. Though the woman was the cause of sin, yet she shall be saved, not only the virgin and the continent, but also the married woman, even if she never ceased from the work of marriage, if, advancing through the begetting of children, she departs from this world. If they continue in faith and love and sanctification, so as to know no other man besides their own husband. With sobriety. That is, temperance, so as to use even their own husband temperately.
3.1: 3.1 He desires a good work. A work, not a dignity; labor, not delights; not to grow in eminence but to decrease in humility, to become the servant and minister of men for Christ's sake, so that even leaving Rachel of comely face, yet not forsaking her, he enters in to Leah of the bleary eyes with Jacob, and with Moses descends from the mountain to the plains, from the leisure of contemplation to the labor of action.
3.2: 3.2 Blameless. The same as to Titus, without crime. A thing almost against nature, to be without sin: but let one be chosen in comparison with whom the rest of the flock may be called. The husband of one wife, etc. That is, married once after baptism. For if before it he also had a wife who died, it is not imputed to him, for to one wholly new neither fornications nor other things that were before now count against him. Sober, etc. The ministers of the temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, and that the sense may be vigorous and always keen.
3.3: 3.3 Not covetous. Seeking nothing beyond food and clothing.
3.6: 3.6 Lest being puffed up with pride. The priest of a moment does not know humility, the measures of persons, or to despise himself; he has not fasted, not wept, not corrected himself, not given to the poor. Into arrogance, which is the ruin of the devil, fall those who in a moment, not yet disciples, become masters. But he must, etc. This clause suits the beginning, that he be blameless not only to those of his household but to outsiders, Jews, Gentiles, heretics, that those who speak ill of religion may not dare to speak ill of its right.
3.10: 3.10 No one, etc. A crime is a grave sin, most worthy of accusation and condemnation.
3.15: 3.15 The Church. The calling together of many to the worship of the one God. The pillar of truth. Well sustaining the truth in itself, that it not fall, though it be afflicted.
3.16: 3.16 Seen by angels. What was hidden is made known to the angels not only in God, but here too it appears to them when it is accomplished and made public; therefore he is said to have appeared to the angels, no longer in the form of humility but in power; he who was first seen lowly, death having been conquered, appeared in majesty, that the angels, recognizing the mystery which before lay hidden, declared in the flesh, bending the knee to him might as to God give thanks, because they had learned the truth. In the world. That the perfidy of the world may not be able to deserve pardon for its error. As the Lord says of the Jews: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin, etc., John 15.
4.1: 4.1 But the Spirit manifestly says. What the Holy Spirit revealed to him as to come, for the instruction and caution of the Church; he does not keep silent, saying that there will be men of pestilential doctrine, that the Church, forewarned, may be careful not to be circumvented by such men, as if he said: So worthy is the house of God, but the Spirit manifestly says. And therefore, on account of its sublimity, do not lay aside care.
4.2: 4.2 Seared. A cautery is an iron, so called from taking care.
4.3: 4.3 Which God created. This is the doctrine of the saints, that of the demons.
4.5: 4.5 It is sanctified. Food becomes holy and wholesome, not harmful to soul or body; the word sanctifies, prayer obtains, but the devil tempts through food.
4.8: 4.8 For bodily. It is given to understand here that Timothy exercised himself in vigils, fasts, prayers and good works, not so intent on works of mercy. Godliness, which works good to the brethren and avails to deserve God.
4.11: 4.11 Command these things. He admonishes him that his progress in all things be an example to others, that in a young man there may appear admirable and grave discipline, that his acts excuse him, and he be held not as a youth but as an elder, and that the older be ashamed if they do not show themselves grave after his pattern in conduct and morals.
4.14: 4.14 Prophecy. He called prophecy the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he foreknew what he would do about this man and the rest. Therefore he says: Which was given you by prophecy: because by the revelation of the Spirit the Apostle knew that Timothy was worthy of episcopal honor. Of the presbytery. For of the presbyters, because there cannot be fewer than three. And he calls the presbyter a bishop; or because one lays on hands with the rest assenting.
5.1: 5.1 Rebuke not an elder. Lest, taking it ill to be corrected by a younger man, he be more exasperated than helped.
5.2: 5.2 As sisters. That seeing themselves admonished out of love, they may more easily correct themselves. In all chastity. In speaking with young women a young man is rightly admonished about chastity.
5.3: 5.3 Honor widows that are widows indeed. That is, those who are destitute of the help of all their own, and who cannot work with their hands, whom poverty weakens and age wears out: whose hope is God, and whose whole work is prayer.
5.4: 5.4 To parents. The parents are the same as the children and grandchildren above. Hence even in worldly law a parent is commanded to succeed a parent by degree. To whom we render a mutual turn, when we have been brought up by fathers and nourish others by the same law.
5.5: 5.5 Desolate, let her hope. Seeing that she has support from no side, she is devoted with her whole soul to God, from whom alone she hopes for help of life and salvation.
5.6: 5.6 She that lives in pleasures. It is a kind of imposture to wish to have the honor of a widow and not to obey God, and to do one thing and profess another, when she professes religion.
5.8: 5.8 Has no care. Care is owed to parents, as Jesus commended his mother to John.
5.10: 5.10 Feet. AUGUSTINE, Tract 58 on John. Let us do to one another humbly what the Most High did humbly, etc., down to the effect of humility is confirmed. Of the saints. Of whom, I ask? Of those who are in tribulation, not simply of the saints: for they can be holy, and yet be cherished by all with the highest service. Do not follow those abounding in plenty of goods, but the afflicted and those unknown to many. Do not give these things to the prelate of the Church to distribute; minister yourself, that you may receive the reward not only of the expense but of the service: give with your own hands, sow the furrow of piety yourself.
5.11: 5.11 Avoid. That is, do not care for their vows of chastity so far as to receive them to be sustained by the alms of the Church.
5.12: 5.12 Having. AUGUSTINE, On the Good of Widowhood, chs. 8, 9, 10. In the conjugal bond, if chastity is preserved, damnation is not feared, etc., down to every such one is like Lot's wife, who looked back. They have made void. Even if not by marrying, yet by willing: not that marriage is condemned, but the breach of the purpose, and the broken faith of the vow is condemned, and the will that departs from the purpose is damnable, whether marriage follows or not.
5.15: 5.15 Have turned back after Satan. From that excellent purpose of widowhood or virginal chastity, looking back, they fell and perished.
5.17: 5.17 Let the elders who rule well. Here he treats of the honor of presbyters, as if to say: What I said about widows observe: and this also command about presbyters, that presbyters who preside well in life and doctrine be held worthy.
5.19: 5.19 Against a presbyter receive not an accusation, etc. He who corrects is usually not loved, and so, occasion being taken, is easily accused. Against this he warns that an accusation against a presbyter is not to be received easily.
5.20: 5.20 Before all, etc. AUGUSTINE, sermon 16 on the Words of the Lord. Sometimes you ought to rebuke the sinner between you and him alone, etc., down to but when the sin is public, it must be rebuked publicly.
5.21: 5.21 I charge you before God. That is, let God be my witness that I have saved my own soul in regard to you; take care.
5.23: 5.23 Drink no longer water, etc. Because he had admonished about chastity, on this occasion he forbids immoderate abstinence, which he himself had entered upon.
5.24: 5.24 Some men's sins, etc. Because he had said nothing is to be done without prejudgment, he determines where prejudgment is necessary and where not, dividing goods and evils into manifest and hidden, as if to say: examination is needed because, just as some things are manifest which need not be examined, so some are hidden, about which no judgment can be made without prior examination. Manifest. He says this of those about which it is clear in what spirit they are done; these go before to judgment, because if judgment follows them it is not rash. They follow after. As the evils that are hidden will not lie hid in their time when the time of Christ shall come to manifest them: so also with good things. Of these therefore let us judge: let the others be left to the judgment of God.
6.1: 6.1 Whoever. It is to be known that some had preached a freedom common to all in Christ. Which is true of spiritual freedom, but not of carnal, as they understood it: therefore the Apostle speaks against them here, bidding servants be subject to their masters. Let not the servants demand what is said of the Hebrews, that they serve six years and be dismissed free for nothing, which is mystical.
6.4: 6.4 Proud. For pride, not reason, leads him, when to seek favor he breaks out into conflict, which is avoided by the meek and good. Sick. For by refusing the faith he does not wholly die, nor grow strong to the knowledge of the truth, but as with repeated attacks he languishes over questions and strifes of words. Questions. The question was whether he was a servant, since all sprang from the same fathers and Christ has redeemed all.
6.9: 6.9 For they that will. This is said to those who wish and are not rich, that they not desire. To the rich something else is said already, namely not to be proud, but to give to the poor. They fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, because the root of all evils, etc. There is no kind of evil that does not sometimes proceed from covetousness, because covetousness is the root of all evils.
6.10: 6.10 Covetousness. In the Greek it is. If therefore avarice is meant, which is properly the love of money, the species is put for the genus, which is covetousness. With many sorrows. For the avaricious endure the torment of anxiety the more, the more they desire things that either pass away when had, or that they cannot have.
6.11: 6.11 But you, O man, etc. He does not say that he fears this of him, but he knew it would come into the hands of the churches. Flee these things. For nothing is so harsh and so pernicious as for an ecclesiastical man, especially one who holds a high place, to be eager for the riches of this world: because he harms not only himself but others, to whom he gives a contrary pattern. Godliness. Godliness is to condescend to the needy, which the covetous man does not do. Faith. He who has true faith concerning God does not desire to become rich in miseries, nor is the world of more worth to him than God.
6.13: 6.13 I charge you. In Timothy the Apostle speaks to all successors. And Christ Jesus. He exhorts by the example of Christ.
6.15: 6.15 Blessed and only, etc. He says this not of the Father only but of God who is the Trinity itself.
6.16: 6.16 Who only has immortality. He has it by nature, others from him by grace. Inaccessible, which no man. Because no one approaches it of himself, but to whom it is given, it is given by his gift, which the Prophet understood saying: Come to him and be enlightened, Psalm 33, etc.
6.17: 6.17 To the rich of this world. Above he dealt with those who wish to become rich, saying that they fall into temptation and the snare of the devil; here he deals with those who are rich, admonishing them not to hope in riches. And because he said evils come from covetousness, and persuaded against it, lest the rich seem cast away, he determines. Not high-minded. The Apostle did not fear riches, but their disease, that is pride, which is the worm of the rich. Great is the soul that among riches is not tempted by this disease. He is great who does not think himself great because he is rich. But he who therefore thinks himself great is proud, he is needy, he swells in the flesh, bursts in the heart, begs, is puffed up, not full. For enjoyment. For God gives temporal things in this life for use, eternal for enjoyment: the former, that from them we may do good; the latter, that from them we may be made good.
6.19: 6.19 To lay up treasure. For this, imperishable riches are set forth beforehand.
6.20: 6.20 O Timothy. Timothy, precious to God. Precious, God. Profane. As hypostasis is, a word which refers both to person and to substance. Hence the heretics, under the multiplying of this name, wished to bring in three substances. Understand profane voices to be those which are against religion; others are not to be avoided.
6.21: 6.21 Which some professing have erred concerning the faith, etc. For these love nothing so much as to promise knowledge, and to deride as ignorance the faith in true things (which little ones are commanded to believe).
